episode_thesis: Toby Crabel (short-term systematic futures, recorded 23 March 2026) argues that edges do not vanish because they are published but because market structure and participants change: the opening range breakout he wrote up in 1989 decayed mainly because 24-hour trading removed the open as a reference point, and today large algorithmic traders use the liquidity at obvious highs and lows, so reversals are more common than follow-through. His response is continuous adaptation (about 10% of the portfolio changed each year, shorter holds, balanced generalised mean-reversion and momentum strategies, heavy execution investment, volume-price research) rather than trusting any single optimised model.

speakers.name: Toby Crabel
speakers.role: Founder of Crabel Capital Management (short-term systematic futures, since the late 1980s); author of the opening range breakout book (1989); former Niederhoffer associate

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are non-linear and only probabilistic, so anything can happen, and AI cannot give a reliable five-minute forecast; the mood among systematic and discretionary traders is humility.
worldview_premises.support: Experience of the 23 March 2026 gold and silver move and general principle.

worldview_premises.premise: Opening range breakout was a foundational short-term momentum edge: Chicago bond floor traders faded an 8-tick move off the open but followed beyond it; it measures intraday momentum, a large factor, and he kept the opposite view (mean reversion) learned from Niederhoffer.
worldview_premises.support: Own history from the 1980s and 1990s; book published 1989.

worldview_premises.premise: Very short-term trading is viable only when transaction costs are near zero; he moved from trend following to shorter-term trading because his partner's account paid no commissions, and the firm's time frame harks back to zero-commission days.
worldview_premises.support: Own story; the exchange-floor mentality of day traders.

worldview_premises.premise: An edge can persist after publication and be lost only when structure or participants change: the decade after his 1989 book was among the best ever for opening range breakout, and decay came from 24-hour trading, which he first saw with US Treasury night sessions in the 1980s; an early S&P pit pattern that quadrupled an account in two months vanished when institutions entered.
worldview_premises.support: Own history of the strategy and of the S&P pit pattern; no data series shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets that still trade a defined primary session (palm oil, Brazilian markets) show much better opening range breakout results, supporting the explanation that 24-hour trading destroyed the open as a reference point.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison across markets from his own observation; no figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend days are less frequent than before because liquidity is positioned against momentum, pushing strategies toward mean reversion; there are many more intraday reversals (for example a new overnight low followed by a large rally) and fewer follow-through days than in a long time.
worldview_premises.support: 50 years of observation, the day's price action, and a statistic that follow-through after a higher low fell from about 62% to 58%.

worldview_premises.premise: Large algorithmic market makers and big traders use activity beyond prior-day highs and lows to enter and exit; volatile liquidity events are an opportunity for them, and breaks of obvious levels are often traps built on fearful traders liquidating.
worldview_premises.support: 23 March 2026 gold and silver reversal on 5-10 times normal volume, with large contracts trading ten minutes before Iran-talk headlines (he notes there is no confirmation).

worldview_premises.premise: Large volume outside prior ranges signals opportunity for big players, and volume matters more now than he can recall; the Wyckoff 1930s study of the New York Times index in a volatile bear market resembles today.
worldview_premises.support: Wyckoff historical study; recollection ('I may be wrong').

worldview_premises.premise: The relationship between volume and price is under-researched; many stick to price alone, and volume is hard to use consistently because its scale has changed enormously (15 million NYSE shares a day was huge in the 1970s).
worldview_premises.support: Own research experience; databases so deep that each answered question raises about 50 more.

worldview_premises.premise: Wyckoff's effort versus result remains valid: effort is volume and result is the price range; high volume with a narrow range at a dead stop shows a large trader absorbing flow, so after a rally it is a poor place to buy and at a low someone is standing in front of the move.
worldview_premises.support: A 100-year-old concept applied to current price action, with no test shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Charts show what is going on and the human mind still extracts information from them better than a computer, so the firm quantifies visual observations to detect market changes and still has to tell the computer what to do; technical analysis lacks a philosophical justification, which is the subject of his next book (a cognitive element).
worldview_premises.support: Own practice and preference; no evidence offered.

worldview_premises.premise: Old portfolios do not work as well as current ones, so markets evolve; the firm changes 10% or more of its portfolio every year, and without such changes the portfolio of 5-10 years ago would have put it out of business.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's backtests of old portfolios; no figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Uncertainty has grown, especially in the last few years, so outlier moves catch portfolios more easily and do more damage, although the basic concepts remain valid and there is room for new ones.
worldview_premises.support: Observation, no quantification.

worldview_premises.premise: Basic momentum strategies have deteriorated by 4-5 points of hit rate (still above 50%) because options traders and pod groups compress volatility; markets are also jumpy and news-prone, so the firm's average hold shortened from about 36 hours to less.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's research group findings (led by its CEO, Mike Blumaden in the captions); no tables.

worldview_premises.premise: Over-optimisation is self-deception: generalised strategies hold up (some 1990s strategies still run) and optimised strategies look better on paper only; he looks for strategies that could last 50 years.
worldview_premises.support: A year in the late 1990s when four of the top five strategies were generalised ones.

worldview_premises.premise: Execution is a main source of edge: execution quality has improved by multiples in 20-25 years and slippage is at the best level in the firm's history; S&P futures book depth fell from about 500 contracts to about 20 at the touch while volume rose, so orders must be split and the method is more cagey.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's slippage reports.

worldview_premises.premise: High-frequency firms are the liquidity backbone, like the old floor traders; they spend millions for a few microseconds of speed, whereas the firm prefers cheaper execution edge (with some frustrating nuances).
worldview_premises.support: Memory of floor traders; ledger correction says he does not claim short-term managers' alpha is untouched.

worldview_premises.premise: Short-term strategies are hard to replicate because of nuance and heavy execution investment (they are a higher-cost product), while trend following is easier to replicate, and the firm's trend product has done slightly better than replication.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's own comparison of trend products; no figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Capacity is judged by net dollars per contract against execution cost, and matters far more for very short-term trading than for 5-10 day holds.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's practice.

worldview_premises.premise: AI and genetic algorithms accelerate quantification, so short-term trading becomes more competitive as everyone uses every tool; AI coding tools (Codex and others) let staff build and program verbally, which he expects to be the next major change cutting development and operating cost.
worldview_premises.support: Firm-wide mandate by the CEO including the back office.

worldview_premises.premise: The current environment resembles the 1970s (debasement, gold and silver, profitable trend following, large abrupt moves) but is bigger and global; markets are as tough as in 40-50 years for systematic traders although he expects them to improve, and he suspects a further unidentified factor.
worldview_premises.support: Historical analogy; personal gold and silver coin holdings and a life insurance policy that has lost 95% against gold.

worldview_premises.premise: Momentum makes money even though he does not like it personally, but it is hard to trade on a discretionary basis because the market moves slowly during the process, so it suits systematic rules.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience.

worldview_premises.premise: Opening range breakout took 8-10 more years to decay after he added mean reversion to offset it; changes are glacial, and replacement reference points (previous close and overnight movement, previous-day highs and lows, 24-hour session range) still work, less strongly than the old opening range.
worldview_premises.support: His own portfolio experience after working with Niederhoffer.

worldview_premises.premise: Model retirement and allocation depend on recognising individual strategy deterioration and the environment that is changing it.
worldview_premises.support: Firm's research group practice.

decision_process.practice: Run a balanced mix of six primary mean-reversion and six primary momentum strategies, each uncorrelated with the others.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The statistic that follow-through after a higher low fell from about 62% to 58% is quoted from memory with no definition of the sample, horizon or period.
The statement that opening range breakout was as bad in the last two or three years as in an earlier worst period depends on a garbled year in the captions; 'worst in decades' is not what he said.
The hit-rate deterioration of 4-5 points has no baseline and no horizon; the 36-hour average hold is from memory.

The 23 March 2026 claims (5-10 times normal volume, contracts traded before the Iran headlines, daily moves larger than ever) are an in-the-moment reading with no confirmation; he says himself that the pre-announcement trades are unconfirmed and the size of moves can be verified.

He says conditions are the toughest for systematic traders in 40-50 years and that old portfolios fail, yet reports that trend products did very well in March 2026 and that execution slippage is at a record best; the sources of the difficulty are not reconciled.
Wyckoff effort versus result: the correction notes the decline case means someone is standing in front of the move (do not chase the decline), not simply 'do not buy'; the claim is untested here.
The 200-day moving average remark is the host's inference, not Crabel's; the ledger had attributed it to Crabel.

He argues a known edge persists after publication, while describing the S&P pit pattern as vanishing within two months of institutions entering; the difference is attributed to structure and participants, not to publicity, but no test separates them.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Crabel's inputs are reference-point behaviour (previous close, overnight movement, prior-day highs and lows, 24-hour range), extraordinary volume (especially at the start of a regional session or outside prior ranges), volume-price effort versus result, and the ratio of follow-through to reversals; horizons are minutes to a few days (average hold under 36 hours). Macro context: currency debasement and a 1970s-like regime favour large abrupt moves and trend following; gold and silver holding after 23 March 2026 would imply higher prices over three to six months.
reader_inferences: (reader) Crabel's explanation of decay is about reference points and who supplies liquidity, not about crowding: an edge survives publication if the structure that created it survives, which implies that edge half-lives should be estimated from market structure changes (sessions, participants) rather than from the age of the strategy.

(reader) The fall of follow-through from 62% to 58% and of momentum hit rates by 4-5 points suggest the edge in short-term systematic trading is a few percentage points of hit rate, which makes execution cost and slippage first-order, consistent with his heavy execution investment.
(reader) His balanced mean-reversion and momentum portfolio and 10% annual turnover form an insurance against regime shifts in market microstructure; the cost is unknown from the conversation.

(reader) His bullish gold and silver call is explicitly conditional on the lows holding and is not backed by the firm's systematic process, so it is better read as a discretionary view than as a signal of the firm.
